<reason>B built the cleaner, more consistent path to victory. It forced A to concede new-build delivers roughly nothing in-window — half the motion's mechanism — and weaponized that concession in every later speech. Its "calendar cheat" catch on A's 20-year amortization was never escaped: A4 kept spreading relicensing costs over the plant's remaining life despite the ten-year frame being pressed twice. B also kept the "reduce vs. stasis" asymmetry alive (renewables displace fossil running now; extension needs a hypothetical closure). A's closing was the debate's single best move — the clean-backfill opportunity-cost turn — but it arrived late, and B answered it directly: the "enabler, not reducer" catch exposed that A's final architecture cast nuclear as supporting the renewable dollar rather than out-reducing it, and the clean-backfill fork was anchored in cost arguments (bailouts, market verdict) live since the opening. Both sides showed strong epistemic discipline: no fake citations, plausible approximations, honest concessions (B on outage duration, A on new-build). A's firming-dilution argument stayed contested but never decisive. B made the debate easier to decide on the motion's own terms.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.6's "calendar cheat" catch (20-year amortization vs. the 10-year window) was a wound A never closed, but the decisive exchange was the closing sequence: A's clean-backfill opportunity-cost turn (renewables can't both backfill closures and displace fossil) met B's "enabler not reducer" reframe plus the zero-incremental-tons fork — B converted A's strongest argument into a concession of the motion's comparative claim.</best_rebuttal>
